opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it goes back quite a few years now. After working on computer vision — Inception, batch normalization, and the adversarial examples work — I had this growing feeling that perception was, in a sense, becoming a solved problem, or at least that the trajectory was clear. Throw more data and compute at it, and it gets better. But what was really missing was the ability of these systems to reason: to chain together steps, to verify their own conclusions, to do something that looks like what a mathematician does when they prove a theorem.

So around 2015, 2016, I started to shift my focus toward formal mathematics and theorem proving. Mathematics is a really nice testbed for reasoning, because it's a domain where you can actually check whether you're right. You have formal proof assistants like HOL Light, Lean, Coq, and if the system produces a proof, the checker tells you unambiguously whether it's correct. That gives you a very clean signal, which is something you don't get in most natural-language tasks.

That's what led to work like DeepMath, and later HOList, where we built an environment and benchmark around HOL Light so that neural networks could learn to do premise selection and guide proof search. And from there I became very interested in what I call autoformalization: the idea that you could take the enormous body of informal mathematics, papers and textbooks written in natural language, and have a system translate it into formal, machine-checkable form. If you can do that, then you have a closed loop. The system can read mathematics, formalize it, try to prove things, verify them, and learn from its own successes and failures. That's a path toward a kind of self-improving reasoning system.

I made a somewhat public bet a few years ago that we would see AI reaching superhuman mathematician-level ability within a decade or so, and people thought it was quite optimistic at the time. But I think the progress we've seen with large language models has, if anything, made me more confident. Language models gave us the missing piece: the ability to work with informal mathematics and natural language at scale. Combine that with the rigor of formal verification, and I think you get something very powerful.

So in short, the conviction that reasoning is the next frontier pushed me away from pure perception and toward mathematics, formal verification, and the interface between informal and formal reasoning. And I still believe that's where some of the most important breakthroughs are going to come from, not just for math itself, but because verified reasoning is the foundation for trustworthy AI more generally, whether in software verification, science, or anything else where correctness really matters.

r001.rationale: The response describes neural networks guiding formal proof search and autoformalization translating informal mathematics into machine-checkable form, connecting informal and formal reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's been the thread running through pretty much everything I've done for the last decade. I think it started around 2014, 2015, when it became clear to me that deep learning was going to handle perception extremely well. We had image recognition basically working, and the question for me became: what is the hard thing that is left? And the answer I kept coming back to was reasoning. Not pattern matching on a huge pile of examples, but the ability to take a few premises and derive something genuinely new from them, something you've never seen before.

So I made a somewhat unusual choice at the time. Instead of continuing on vision, where I had been fairly successful with things like Inception and batch normalization, I moved toward formal mathematics and automated theorem proving. People thought it was a strange detour. But my reasoning was that mathematics is the cleanest possible testbed. In math, you have a precise notion of what a correct step is. You can verify it mechanically. There's no ambiguity about whether the model got it right or just sounded plausible. If you want to study reasoning in isolation, without all the noise of natural language, formal math is where you get the crispest signal.

That's what led to the work on HOList and the autoformalization direction, trying to get neural networks to prove theorems in interactive proof assistants, and eventually trying to translate informal mathematics into formal statements automatically. The long-term bet was that if you could build a system that reads math papers and turns them into verified formal proofs, you'd essentially have a system that can reason, because you've grounded it in something that can't be faked.

What's interesting is how the landscape shifted. For a long time I was arguing that scale alone wouldn't give you reasoning, that you needed some kind of search or verification loop on top of learned intuition. And then large language models came along and showed that a surprising amount of reasoning-like behavior does emerge from scale. So I had to update. But I don't think it invalidated the core view. If anything, I'd say the current direction, where people combine language models with search, with self-verification, with reinforcement learning on reasoning traces, that's very much the picture I had in mind. Learned intuition proposing steps, and some mechanism checking them.

So the way it shaped my research is that I always asked myself: does this bring us closer to systems that can discover things, rather than just recall them? And if the answer was no, I generally wasn't that interested, even if it was a good short-term result.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes using neural networks for theorem proving in formal proof assistants and for translating informal mathematics into formal statements, connecting formal and informal reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I’ve come to think of reasoning as one of the central problems we need to solve. Deep learning is very good at learning patterns, but reasoning asks for something more: combining what you know through a sequence of steps, and being able to check whether those steps are actually valid.

That pushed me toward mathematical reasoning and automated theorem proving. Mathematics gives you a particularly clean setting for studying this, because you can specify a problem precisely and verify a proposed proof. You’re not limited to asking whether an answer looks plausible; you can check it.

What interests me is the interaction between learning and search. Learning can guide you toward promising steps, while a formal system can tell you whether those steps are correct. My hope is that working on that combination will help us build systems that can tackle increasingly difficult reasoning problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining learning with formal verification, but it does not clearly identify neural networks as the means of connecting formal and informal reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I came to think that reasoning was one of the most important missing pieces in machine learning. We had made tremendous progress in perception, but recognizing patterns and carrying out a long, reliable chain of reasoning are quite different problems. I wanted to understand how we could bridge that gap.

That pushed me toward mathematics and formal theorem proving. There, you can state a problem precisely, and you have a way to check whether a proposed solution is correct. A neural network can suggest a step or guide a search, while a proof checker provides very reliable feedback. That combination seemed particularly promising to me.

The broader motivation is not just to build a system that proves mathematical theorems. It is to understand how learning and reasoning can reinforce each other—how a system can discover useful abstractions and then use them to solve increasingly difficult problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes neural networks guiding formal theorem proving with proof-checker feedback, but it does not describe connecting formal and informal reasoning.
